title: Gradual Release (I Do / We Do / You Do)
preview: Teach in three moves: you do it first, you do it together, they do it alone. Responsibility shifts from teacher to student step by step.

body.summary: Gradual Release (often called "I Do / We Do / You Do") is a simple three-phase structure. First, YOU model the problem completely while students watch. Then, you solve one TOGETHER — the group contributes ideas but you're still steering. Finally, students try one ON THEIR OWN while you watch. Each phase pulls back a little support, like taking the training wheels off a bike one side at a time. It works for any math skill and any age.
body.whenToUse:
Use for any new skill or any skill a student has shown they can't do alone. It's the default move for small-group intervention. It's less useful when students already have the skill and just need practice — in that case, skip straight to "You Do."

Each phase should stay short. If "I Do" takes 10 minutes, you've lost them. Aim for 3-5 minutes per phase.
body.howToImplement:
1. I DO (3-5 min): You solve one problem from start to finish. Students watch and listen.
   Say: "Watch me do this one. Don't write anything yet — just watch how I do it."
   Narrate your steps out loud (see Think-Aloud Modeling strategy).

2. WE DO (3-5 min): You solve the next problem TOGETHER.
   Say: "Now let's do one together. I'll start, but I'm going to ask you for the next step."
   Ask the group at each step: "What do you think I should do next?" and "Why?"
   If no one answers, give them a choice: "Should I add or multiply here?" Yes/no or A/B questions keep momentum.

3. YOU DO (3-5 min): Students solve the next problem alone.
   Say: "Your turn. Do this one on your own. I'll walk around and check your work."
   Do NOT help them. Watch. Take notes on who is stuck.

4. CHECK-IN: After "You Do," ask one student to share how they solved it. If many students got it wrong, GO BACK to "We Do" with a new problem before trying "You Do" again.
body.teacherMoves:
IF students try to jump in during "I Do":
→ Say: "I love that you're thinking! But this one is my turn. I promise you'll get a turn in about 2 minutes."

IF no one answers during "We Do":
→ Give a choice: "Should I add the numbers or multiply them?" Then follow up with "Why did you pick that?"
→ Or say: "Turn to the person next to you for 10 seconds — what should I do next?"

IF most students are wrong during "You Do":
→ Stop. Say: "I saw a lot of us making the same mistake. Let me show you one more example." Go back to "I Do" or "We Do" with a fresh problem.

IF one student gets it, but others don't:
→ Say to the student who got it: "Can you explain your first step to the group?" Then you follow up and reinforce.

IF you only have time for one or two phases:
→ Do "I Do" and "You Do." Skipping "We Do" is better than rushing all three.
body.variations:
TIER 2 (Scaffolded):
Use as described. For extra support in "We Do," write the steps on the board as the group names them. Students can see the thinking AND hear it.

TIER 3 (Heavy Support):
Add a FOURTH step — "You Do Together." Between "We Do" and "You Do," let two students pair up and solve one together before trying solo. This extra scaffold helps students who freeze when asked to work alone.

QUICK VERSION (5 minutes total):
One I Do, one We Do, one You Do. No more than 90 seconds per phase. Useful when you only have a short intervention window.
body.researchBase: Pearson and Gallagher (1983) described the Gradual Release of Responsibility model as a way to shift cognitive load from teacher to student over time. Fisher and Frey (2008) refined it for classroom use. The Institute of Education Sciences Practice Guide for math intervention (Gersten et al., 2009) identifies explicit, systematic instruction with modeling and guided practice as one of the strongest evidence-based practices for struggling learners.
body.inlineTip: Use all three phases for this problem: YOU solve one, then do one TOGETHER with the group, then let students try alone while you watch.
